feedback: If a learner says the figures just increase 'by chance', relink each rise to many-prey-per-predator plus retention.
Confirm the key fact: the environment can hold only a trace while the top of the chain carries a dangerous, potentially lethal dose.

Note that this ladder shows the pattern and case history but is a fixed example: it does not let you vary the dose or test the persistence counterfactual, so pair it with the feeding activity for the mechanism.
Note that the real figures do not rise by exactly ten each step (roughly x12.5, x4, x12.5), so treat the 1/10/100/1000 model as a simplified illustration of the same upward multiplication.
activities.intendedInsight: Real measured concentrations show the toxin is lowest where it enters (water/producers) and highest in the top predator, evidencing the multiplication pattern and its real population-level consequences.
learnerActions: Study a DDT food-chain ladder with real ppm figures at each level: plankton 0.04 ppm -> small fish 0.5 -> large fish 2 -> osprey 25.
For each level, answer 'why is this one higher than the one below it?' and specifically 'why is the osprey's so high?'

Examine the peregrine/osprey egg case and connect the high top-predator concentration to eggshell thinning and population collapse (Silent Spring, 1962, raised alarm about pesticide harm to birds; the eggshell-thinning link was established by later research).
Calculate or estimate roughly how many times more concentrated the osprey is than the plankton (about 25 / 0.04, i.e. ~625x), and state what that means for risk.
activities.title: Read the real DDT concentration ladder

feedback: If a learner says 'the small fish are worst affected because the poison gets weaker higher up', reverse the intuition: the toxin is retained and summed, so it concentrates upward.
If a learner says 'the osprey is big and strong so it copes best', point out body size does not clear a persistent toxin; the top predator receives the summed dose and is most, not least, at risk.
If a learner says 'the osprey must be drinking lots of the water', redirect to the feeding route: the toxin enters at the bottom and is concentrated by feeding up the chain.

A full answer names the top predator as most at risk, cites a real case, and reasons about the counterfactual; a partial answer knows toxins are 'worse at the top' and names an example but omits the persistence-plus-many-prey cause.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can independently construct an evidence-based argument that the top predator carries the summed dose of the whole chain because the toxin persists and predators eat many prey — and can reason about the break-down counterfactual.
learnerActions: Respond to the diagnostic scenario: 'A pesticide washes into a lake at a tiny concentration that is harmless in the water itself. Yet the fish-eating ospreys at the top get sick and their eggs fail. How can the poison be harmless in the water but dangerous in the osprey — and why is it the top predator, not the small fish, that suffers most?'
Construct a short written or spoken argument naming the top predator as most at risk and justifying it via persistence plus accumulation across many prey (MS-LS2-4).
Trace the pathway: show how DDT got from farm crops (via runoff into water) all the way into an osprey at the top of the lake food chain.
Answer the counterfactual: 'If the toxin DID break down quickly inside the body, would it still build up the chain? Why not?'
Explain how bioaccumulation differs from a predator simply eating one very poisonous meal.
Discuss the history using a Rachel Carson / Silent Spring debrief as a prompt for argument and context.
activities.title: Build and argue the case for the top predator

feedback: If a learner confuses toxin with energy, re-run the energy overlay: energy decreases with each step, persistent toxin increases.
Recognition and calculation checks confirm the pattern but do not by themselves elicit a full constructed argument; use them alongside the argument activity.
For the habitat-change evidence point, prompt a concrete worked example (earthworms, beavers) since the toxin case centres on bioaccumulation, not habitat engineering.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure the quantitative pattern and the crucial discrimination that persistent toxin rises while energy falls up the food chain, plus the broader idea that organisms both affect and are affected by their environment.
learnerActions: Predict the concentration in the top predator given figures lower down, and sequence organisms by toxin load.
Answer 'why is the water low but the eagle high?' and perform a calculation multiplying concentration up the levels.
Answer a discrimination question contrasting toxin (rises up the chain) with energy (falls up the chain).
Separately, explain how organisms can change their habitat (e.g. earthworms aerating soil, beavers creating wetlands) to address the full 'affect their environment' objective.
activities.title: Check the reasoning (including the energy-vs-toxin discrimination)
